Title revised: Paul's Defense Before Agrippa / 아그립바 앞에서의 변론
paragraphs: Agrippa spoke directly to Paul: "Go ahead — tell us your side." Paul took his stand and told his story. "I can't think of anyone, King Agrippa, I'd rather defend myself against these Jewish accusations before than you — you know Jewish customs and all our internal disputes so well."

"Since my youth, my whole life has been lived among my own people in Jerusalem. Practically every Jew in town who watched me grow up — and if they were brave enough they'd tell you to your face — knows I lived as a strict Pharisee, the most demanding branch of our religion. It's because I believed it and took it seriously — committing myself heart and soul to what God promised our ancestors, the very same hope the twelve tribes have clung to day and night all these centuries — it's because I've held on to this tested, proven hope that the Jews are dragging me into court. They should be the ones on trial here, not me! I honestly can't see why believing that God raises the dead is a crime."

"I'll admit I didn't always hold this view. For a while I thought it was my duty to fight this Jesus of Nazareth with everything I had. Armed with full authority from the chief priests, I threw these believers — I had no idea they were God's people! — into Jerusalem jails left and right, and whenever a vote came up, I voted to execute them. I raged through their synagogues, bullying them into cursing Jesus — a one-man wrecking crew obsessed with wiping these people out. Then I started in on towns outside Jerusalem."

"One day, on my way to Damascus — armed as always with papers from the chief priests authorizing my mission — right in the middle of the day, a blaze of light brighter than the sun poured out of the sky onto me and my companions. Oh, King, it was blinding! We fell flat on our faces. Then I heard a voice in Hebrew: 'Saul, Saul, why are you trying to destroy me? Why do you keep fighting against me?'"

"I said, 'Who are you, Master?' The voice answered, 'I am Jesus, the One you're hunting like an animal. But now, get up — I have a job for you. I've handpicked you to be my servant and witness to what happened today, and to what I'm going to show you."

"'I'm sending you to open the eyes of the outsiders, so they can see the difference between darkness and light and choose light — see the difference between Satan and God and choose God. I'm sending you to offer them forgiveness of sins and a place in the family, inviting them into the company of everyone who begins truly living by believing in me.'"

"What could I do, King Agrippa? I couldn't just walk away from a vision like that! I became an obedient believer on the spot. I started preaching this life-change — this radical turn to God and what it means in everyday life — right there in Damascus, then in Jerusalem and the surrounding countryside, and from there to the whole world."

"It's because of this 'whole world' part that the Jews grabbed me in the Temple that day and tried to kill me. They want to keep God to themselves. But God has stood by me, just as he promised, and here I am saying what I've been saying to anyone who'll listen, king or child. And everything I'm saying lines up completely with what the prophets and Moses said would happen: first, the Messiah had to die; second, raised from the dead, he would be the first rays of God's daylight shining on people far and near — the godless and the God-fearing alike."
That was too much for Festus. He burst out: "Paul, you're out of your mind! Too many books, too much staring into space! Snap out of it — come back to reality!"

But Paul held his ground. "With all due respect, Your Honor Festus, I'm not crazy. What I'm saying is true and sane. The king knows what I'm talking about — I'm sure none of this sounds crazy to him. He's known about it all for a long time. This wasn't done in some dark corner, you know. You believe the prophets, don't you, King Agrippa? Don't answer — I know you believe."
But Agrippa did answer: "Keep this up much longer and you'll talk me into becoming a Christian!"
Paul, chains and all, answered, "That's my prayer — sooner or later — that not only you but everyone here today would become what I am. Minus, of course, these chains!"

The king and the governor, along with Bernice and their advisors, got up and went into the next room to discuss what they'd heard. They quickly agreed Paul was innocent, saying, "There's nothing about this man that deserves prison, let alone death."
Agrippa told Festus, "He could be set free right now if he hadn't appealed to Caesar."
title: Paul's Defense Before Agrippa
